paragraphs: Remembering a spoken list requires retaining both the items and their order. This paper proposes a neural implementation of the articulatory loop, a short-term memory mechanism involving speech sounds and rehearsal. Its central proposal is a repeatable signal that changes over time, giving each presented item a temporal context that can later help retrieve it.

Items become connected to context signals and phonemes through Hebbian learning, with both short-term and long-term changes in connection strength. During presentation, speech sounds activate items. During recall, context and phonemic feedback reactivate them. Competition selects one item at a time, while temporary inhibition of the winner helps the network move on to another item.

An approximate analysis assumes Gaussian noise during recall and calculates error probabilities. The model accounts for how errors vary with list position, list length, word length, sound similarity, grouping, and familiarity. Its significance is that these different memory effects are explained through a shared retrieval mechanism, which the authors also propose as a foundation for studying rehearsal and vocabulary acquisition.
neurips-1994-a-solvable-connectionist-mo.tldr: A neural model explains ordered verbal recall through temporal context, speech-sound associations, competition, and temporary inhibition.

paragraphs: Searching an image at several resolutions can save work: a coarse view guides where to examine finer detail. The difficulty is that small, low-resolution objects may lose the features needed to recognize them. This paper addresses that problem by using contextual objects that remain visible and are associated with the target.

The neural networks can receive context explicitly, or learn to detect useful contextual objects themselves. In the second case, the person configuring the system need not identify those objects in advance. The method also uses Integrated Feature Pyramids, which preserve information about fine image structure within low-resolution representations, allowing coarse searches to use more than blurred appearance.

Hierarchical neural systems demonstrate the approach by finding groups of buildings in aerial photographs of farmland. The stated result is that context improves searching at resolutions where the targets themselves are hard to distinguish. Combining evidence across scales makes search more efficient, and the multiresolution approach also gives rise to a natural way of selecting exemplars.
neurips-1994-coarse-to-fine-image-search.tldr: Context and multiresolution features help neural networks locate targets even when coarse images hide their distinguishing details.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether a neural network can acquire grammatical structure simply by encountering grammatical sentences. Its input comes from a simple phrase-structure grammar that includes number agreement, differences in verb transitivity, and recursively constructed noun phrases. These features require learning relationships among words and larger phrases, rather than merely recording which words occur.

The network self-organizes without corrective teaching or predefined task goals. Its design draws on the idea that a frequently encountered sequence can become a single informational unit, or chunk. Classification networks organize words and phrases into categories, while the overall system produces explicit symbol-categorization and phrase-structure rules.

The reported simulations show grammar induction in this structured setting. The contribution is both a learning procedure based only on positive examples and a representation that makes the acquired grammatical rules explicit. The setting matters: the evidence concerns sentences generated by the supplied simple grammar. Within that setting, the work connects exposure to recurring sequences with the emergence of organized syntactic knowledge.
neurips-1994-grammar-learning-by-a-self-.tldr: A self-organizing network learns explicit word categories and phrase rules from grammatical example sentences without corrective teaching.

paragraphs: This paper develops an analogue neural-network chip that classifies the shapes of electrical signals recorded inside the heart. The intended setting is an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, where power consumption and physical size impose strict constraints. Analogue circuitry addresses those constraints, while the network architecture reduces the effects of circuit noise, drift, and offsets.

The design uses a multilayer perceptron with 10 inputs, six hidden units, and three outputs. Digital storage holds its weights on the chip, a bucket-brigade input supplies the cardiac signal, and an output competition circuit selects the winning response. Training includes the hardware in the loop and places a commercial defibrillator in the signal-processing path.

Tests across different patients achieved true-positive and true-negative detection above 90% for dangerous rhythms described as undetectable by then-current defibrillators. The chip uses a 1.2-micrometre CMOS process, occupies 2.2 by 2.2 millimetres, and reports maximum average power below 200 nanowatts. Together, the findings connect classification performance with the practical requirements of implantable hardware.
neurips-1994-iceg-morphology-classificat.tldr: An ultra-low-power analogue neural chip classifies intracardiac signal shapes to identify dangerous rhythms in an implantable-defibrillator setting.

paragraphs: Objects in the same category can have substantially different shapes. A deformable model handles this variability by allowing its shape to change as it is fitted to an observation. This makes the approach attractive for recognizing nonrigid objects, but fitting introduces a difficult search problem: the system must find a configuration that matches the data.

The paper uses a neural network to supply a better initial configuration for that search. The network therefore contributes an informed starting point, after which the deformable model can be fitted. This division of work connects a learned prediction with a representation designed to accommodate differences in shape.

The method is demonstrated on character recognition, and the authors report a significant reduction in search time. The finding highlights the importance of initialization: improving where fitting begins can make a flexible recognition model more practical to use. The central contribution is a way to reduce the computational burden associated with fitting deformable models to variable examples.
neurips-1994-using-a-neural-net-to-insta.tldr: A neural network supplies better starting configurations for deformable models, significantly reducing fitting time in character recognition.

paragraphs: Hemineglect involves failing to respond to stimuli on the side of space opposite a parietal brain lesion. This paper asks whether a theory originally developed to explain spatial representation can also explain this impairment. In that theory, neurons compute basis functions of sensory inputs, collectively representing position without committing to one particular reference frame.

Such a representation can support nonlinear transformations between sensory information and motor responses, and it is consistent with the response properties of parietal neurons. The authors test its consequences by introducing a simulated lesion. This lets them examine whether damage to the proposed representation produces recognizable patterns of spatial neglect.

The damaged model reproduces three reported features: missing the leftmost lines during line cancellation, deficits spanning multiple reference frames, and neglect organized relative to an object. These results support the basis-function hypothesis by connecting its neural representation to behavioral consequences of damage. The work thus offers a single-cell-level computational account linking ordinary spatial processing with several manifestations of hemineglect.
neurips-1995-a-model-of-spatial-represen.tldr: Simulated damage to a basis-function model of spatial representation reproduces three major features of hemineglect.

paragraphs: This paper approaches motor-failure detection by teaching a neural network what healthy operation looks like. The network is an autoassociator: it learns to reproduce its input. Its training examples are spectra measured from a healthy motor, so successful reconstruction captures regularities in those measurements.

Once trained, the network compares a new spectrum with its reconstruction. The difference provides an anomaly signal. A spectrum resembling healthy examples should be reconstructed well, whereas an unfamiliar pattern associated with a fault can produce a larger error. This makes reconstruction error useful for identifying departures from normal operation.

Laboratory tests show the intended separation: healthy-motor measurements produce small errors, while measurements from a faulty motor produce larger ones. The authors also built a monitoring system around this approach and were testing it at three industrial and commercial sites. The laboratory findings support anomaly detection as a basis for failure monitoring; the deployment work described in the abstract was still undergoing testing.
neurips-1995-a-neural-network-autoassoci.tldr: A network trained to reconstruct healthy motor spectra detects faults through increased reconstruction error.

paragraphs: Cochlear-implant speech processors must choose which sound channels to use. The spectral-maxima strategy selects channels according to prominent spectral energy, but the paper identifies a problem: sounds can be confused when their distinguishing information lies in high-frequency features. Energy prominence alone may therefore fail to preserve information needed to tell sounds apart.

The proposed system treats channel selection as a pattern-recognition problem. Multilayer perceptrons are trained on labelled speech from multiple speakers. Each network receives energy coefficients from N channels and returns the indices of M selected channels. The learned mapping uses the pattern across the available channels to decide which subset to retain.

The authors compare this strategy with spectral-maxima selection and report significantly better results. The contribution is a learned selection rule that makes speech patterns relevant to the choice of channels. It connects the information used during training with a concrete processing decision: selecting a limited set of channels from a larger representation of the incoming sound.
neurips-1995-a-novel-channel-selection-s.tldr: A neural pattern recognizer improves cochlear-implant channel selection compared with choosing spectral energy maxima.

paragraphs: This paper presents an integrated analogue processor that decomposes and reconstructs continuous signals in the audio frequency range. Its wavelet representation describes a signal at multiple resolutions, providing a way to organize changing temporal information across frequency scales. The hardware performs this processing in real time.

The processor has 16 parallel channels operating at different clock rates. Each combines complex harmonic modulation with Gaussian low-pass filtering, and together the channels produce a multiresolution representation on a logarithmic frequency scale. Different channel rates are therefore part of how the circuit realizes its range of analysis scales.

The implementation combines analogue and digital circuitry, oversampling, and switched-capacitor filters to obtain a wide linear dynamic range while keeping size and power consumption low. The paper reports experiments on the processor and separate component measurements from a single-channel test chip. Its contribution is a physical implementation connecting the mathematical operations of wavelet analysis and reconstruction to compact, real-time signal-processing hardware.
neurips-1995-analog-vlsi-processor-imple.tldr: A compact mixed analogue–digital processor performs real-time audio wavelet decomposition and reconstruction through 16 parallel channels.

paragraphs: An agent facing an opponent must adapt its actions to where that opponent is located. This paper studies that problem in robotic soccer using a memory-based learning technique. The relevant state information is a continuous-valued attribute describing the opponent's position, and the learner uses that information to choose an action.

The central question concerns how useful earlier training remains when situations vary unpredictably. Exact repetition of a training situation would provide a narrow test of adaptation. The experiments instead consider nondeterministic variations around the situations the agent initially encountered, examining whether prior experience still provides an advantage.

The reported result is conditional: when random variations remain within some bound of the initial training conditions, a trained agent performs better than one starting without prior training. This supports the usefulness of remembered experience for nearby variations in an opponent's position. The stated bound is central to the finding, because the demonstrated benefit concerns variation within a range around prior experience.
neurips-1995-beating-a-defender-in-robot.tldr: Memory-based training helps a robotic soccer agent handle bounded random variations in an opponent's position.

paragraphs: An ensemble benefits from networks that are accurate individually and make different mistakes. If their errors occur in different parts of the input space, combining them can be more useful than collecting networks with similar behavior. This paper introduces ADDEMUP to search directly for a set with both accuracy and diversity.

ADDEMUP uses a genetic algorithm. It begins with an initial population and applies genetic operators to create additional networks. Selection retains a set whose members are as accurate as possible while disagreeing with one another as much as possible. The quality of the collection therefore explicitly influences which networks survive.

Experiments on three DNA problems show that ADDEMUP generates ensembles more accurate than several existing approaches. Additional experiments show that available prior knowledge can improve ensemble quality. The findings support treating ensemble construction as a joint search problem: a network's usefulness depends both on its own predictions and on how those predictions complement the other members of the set.
neurips-1995-generating-accurate-and-div.tldr: ADDEMUP uses genetic search to build neural ensembles whose members combine individual accuracy with complementary predictions.

paragraphs: Analogue electronic models of the cochlea require filters whose scales vary exponentially. Building that pattern reliably depends on producing appropriately scaled electrical currents. This paper proposes CMOS-compatible lateral bipolar transistors as a way to generate those currents while improving how closely the circuit elements match their intended relationships.

The transistors are biased along a resistive line with a voltage difference between its ends. That arrangement produces exponentially scaled currents. A key property is independence from the CMOS threshold voltage. The authors explain that this makes the resulting current sources much better matched than sources built from MOS transistors operating in weak inversion.

Measurements from integrated test chips verify the improved matching. The finding matters because a cochlear circuit needs an organized progression of filter scales, making consistency among its current sources directly relevant to its design. The contribution is a device-level implementation choice that supports this progression, backed by measurements of fabricated circuitry.
neurips-1995-improved-silicon-cochlea-us.tldr: CMOS-compatible lateral bipolar transistors improve the matching of exponentially scaled current sources for analogue cochlear models.

paragraphs: Improving a policy requires deciding which actions are better at a given state. The paper starts from the observation that this decision should depend on relative action utilities, called advantages. Nevertheless, existing dynamic-programming methods commonly calculate an absolute utility function as part of the process, even when relative comparisons are the information ultimately needed.

For smooth problems, the authors show that advantages obey two differential consistency conditions. One requires them to be free of curl, a mathematical restriction on how the quantities can vary together. These conditions provide structure that an advantage-based method can enforce rather than treating its local comparisons as unrelated estimates.

The paper shows that enforcing the conditions can support appropriate policy improvement entirely in terms of advantages. Its contribution is a mathematical route from relative evaluations to policy updates without calculating an absolute utility function. The smooth-problem setting matters because the argument relies on differential relationships, connecting the proposed simplification to specific structure in the underlying problem.
neurips-1995-improving-policies-without-.tldr: Differential consistency conditions allow policy improvement using relative action advantages without computing absolute utility.

paragraphs: This paper uses a laterally interconnected self-organizing map, called LISSOM, to prepare handwritten digit images for recognition. The map develops an internal representation before a classifier makes its decision. Its distinctive feature is that connections between map units learn correlations in their activity.

The learned lateral connections have complementary effects. Excitatory connections concentrate activity into local patches, while inhibitory connections reduce redundant activity across the map. Together, these processes produce representations that are easier for a subsequent recognizer, such as a perceptron, to distinguish. The map therefore changes how the input is organized before classification.

On a subset of NIST database 3, the reported recognition rate is 4.0% higher than with a regular self-organizing map and 15.8% higher than recognition directly from raw bitmaps. These comparisons support the value of learned lateral interactions in this setting. The authors present the results as a promising foundation for recognition systems that use LISSOM as their initial representation stage.
neurips-1995-laterally-interconnected-se.tldr: Learned excitation and inhibition in a self-organizing map produce digit representations that improve subsequent recognition.

paragraphs: A moving object can disappear behind another object while continuing along its path. This paper presents a self-organizing network that learns visibility relationships from motion sequences containing disappearance and reappearance. The aim is to represent both what is currently visible and the inferred motion of something temporarily hidden.

For each resolvable motion trajectory, the network develops two parallel chains of excitatory connections. The On chain responds to visible motion. The Off chain maintains a persistent representation of a previously visible stimulus during occlusion. Learning in the Off chain is triggered through disinhibition from the On chain, linking the hidden-motion representation to visible experience.

The two chains can separately learn associations with the depth ordering of objects. This connects prediction through occlusion with information about which object lies in front. The results are related to reported parietal neurons that respond to inferred motion of invisible stimuli. The model offers a learning mechanism through which experience with visibility changes can produce persistent representations of hidden motion.
neurips-1995-learning-to-predict-visibil.tldr: A self-organizing network learns paired pathways for visible motion and the predicted motion of objects hidden by occlusion.

paragraphs: This paper examines how the best way to train an individual learner changes when it belongs to an ensemble. The authors solve a simple model containing linear learners exactly. That setting makes it possible to analyze how regularization, training-set size, and combination weights affect the ensemble's ability to generalize.

For large ensembles, the analysis favors learners with too little regularization, even though those learners overfit their training data. Choosing their training-set sizes appropriately can achieve globally optimal performance within the model. The result shows that optimizing each member in isolation need not produce the best combined predictor.

For smaller ensembles, adjusting the weights used to combine learners can substantially improve generalization, especially when training itself is noisy. Including learners with a broad range of regularization strengths makes this improvement robust to changes in an unknown training-data noise level. These findings establish several ensemble-design tradeoffs within the exactly solved linear setting, including circumstances in which individual overfitting is beneficial.
neurips-1995-learning-with-ensembles-how.tldr: An exact analysis of linear ensembles shows that overfitting members can improve the combined predictor under appropriate training choices.

paragraphs: Sensory-processing systems often recognize a complex entity by combining hypotheses about its component classes. This model-matching stage has computational needs that influence how useful a parallel architecture will be. The paper introduces Single Function Multiple Data, or SFMD, as a model of parallelism suited to this stage of processing.

The proposal is designed as an extension to certain existing Single Instruction Multiple Data architectures. The authors state that SFMD capabilities can be added with little extra hardware and an incremental change to the programming model. That makes the relationship to existing machines central: the proposed functionality builds on an established parallel-computing organization.

The stated benefits include faster model matching, greater flexibility for general-purpose computation, and a broader role in early sensory processing. The contribution therefore concerns both architecture and programmability. By targeting the operation that combines class hypotheses, the paper connects the structure of a recognition problem to a specific extension of the hardware and programming framework used to execute it.
neurips-1995-model-matching-and-sfmd-com.tldr: SFMD extends certain SIMD architectures to accelerate model matching and broaden their sensory-processing capabilities.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether networks of biologically realistic, noisy spiking neurons can perform reliable digital computation in principle. The challenge is that individual elements may behave unreliably, while digital operations require dependable outcomes. The authors address the question through rigorous constructions of networks that simulate established computational systems.

They show how to simulate arbitrary Boolean circuits and finite automata in real time with arbitrarily high reliability. With shunting inhibition, they also construct reliable simulations of threshold gates from very unreliable spiking neurons. Because threshold gates can form multilayer threshold networks, the result extends to that class of neural computation.

The constructions require only weak assumptions about excitatory postsynaptic potential shapes and noise behavior, according to the abstract. Their significance is an existence result: dependable, fast computation is compatible with noisy spiking components under those assumptions. The authors propose this as a possible explanation for complex biological computations occurring within 100 milliseconds, connecting formal computational capability with the speed of neural processing.
neurips-1995-on-the-computational-power-.tldr: Rigorous constructions show that noisy spiking-neuron networks can reliably simulate digital circuits and finite automata in real time.

paragraphs: This paper presents a way to divide sound into segments using the timing of sound beginnings and endings. Its design is inspired by early mammalian auditory processing, particularly features that recordings of neuronal spikes suggest are detected in the cochlear nucleus. The focus is on turning acoustic changes into useful temporal boundaries.

The incoming sound is first separated into frequency bands. Processing within each band emphasizes onsets and offsets, and the resulting signals are compressed. A network of integrate-and-fire neurons then groups these events across time and across frequency channels, bringing together information that was initially represented in separate bands.

Spikes signal the detected onsets and offsets, and their timing determines the sound segmentation. The contribution is a processing chain that links frequency-specific changes to a common representation in event times. Grouping across channels matters because the segmentation decision can draw on related changes throughout the frequency representation, while the spiking network supplies the timing information used to mark boundaries.
neurips-1995-onset-based-sound-segmentat.tldr: An auditory-inspired spiking network segments sound by grouping onset and offset events across time and frequency.

paragraphs: This paper develops a policy-iteration algorithm for improving a motion controller built from harmonic functions. The user specifies the performance criterion to optimize. The task is therefore to adapt the controller toward a chosen objective while preserving the safety properties of its motion guidance.

The method represents value functions as potential distributions over the problem domain and control policies as gradient fields over that same domain. This gives both evaluation and action selection a spatial representation. A central stated property is that every intermediate policy remains intrinsically safe: the adaptation process does not promote collisions.

The algorithm is suitable for efficient implementation on parallel SIMD architectures. Travel-distance minimization illustrates how a user-defined objective can guide its optimization. The contribution brings together three considerations that matter for adaptive motion control: improving a specified performance measure, retaining collision-related safety during the updates themselves, and organizing the computation so it can be carried out efficiently in parallel.
neurips-1995-parallel-optimization-of-mo.tldr: A parallel policy-iteration method optimizes harmonic-function motion controllers while keeping intermediate policies intrinsically safe.

paragraphs: The way information is represented at a neural network's input can strongly affect its accuracy on new examples. Choosing among representations is difficult when each candidate requires expensive training before its quality becomes clear. This paper addresses that selection problem by introducing fast measures of representation quality.

The measures estimate which candidate representation will be best for a given problem. Their purpose is to rank alternatives quickly and accurately, making it more practical to consider a collection of possible inputs. This places representation assessment earlier in the decision process, where it can help direct the costly work of neural-network training.

Experiments on three difficult real-world pattern-recognition problems show more accurate rankings than a previously published measure. The result supports the usefulness of inexpensive quality estimates for comparing representations. The contribution is specifically about predicting the relative usefulness of input choices: it provides a way to make a consequential design decision without relying solely on training a network for every alternative.
neurips-1995-rapid-quality-estimation-of.tldr: Fast quality measures rank candidate neural-network input representations more accurately than an earlier measure on three real-world problems.

paragraphs: This paper approaches visual recognition as a sequence of selective observations. Its motivation is the computational difficulty of completely parallel object recognition, which the abstract characterizes as NP-complete. The proposed compromise combines parallel processing with sequential attention, allowing the system to focus on different parts of an image over time.

Successive fixations sample the image. Each sample is processed and abstracted, contributing to a temporal context that integrates information from multiple observations. The model uses a partially recurrent feedforward network, making earlier observations relevant to the interpretation of later ones. Recognition consequently depends on an accumulated sequence of evidence.

The authors test the model on handwritten digit recognition and describe the results as encouraging. The contribution is a computational account of how selective attention and temporal integration can work together in a recognition system. The digit task provides a concrete test of this idea, showing how a practical recognition problem can be approached through successive image samples and their combined context.
neurips-1995-selective-attention-for-han.tldr: A partially recurrent network recognizes handwritten digits by integrating information from successive selective fixations.

paragraphs: Backpropagation often treats all network weights as one parameter vector, setting aside information about where each connection sits. This paper proposes tempering weight updates according to network structure. The aim is to make learning reflect differences among connections, including how many inputs and outputs their associated nodes have.

The model treats activation and error signals as approximately independent random variables. It matches the characteristic size of weight changes to the scale of residual errors. This allows fan-in and fan-out to influence local learning rates and backpropagated errors. The analysis also gives an upper bound on the global batch-learning rate and leads to different update rules for bias and non-bias weights.

On the deep multilayer family-relations benchmark, tempering speeds convergence by more than an order of magnitude at the optimal learning rate, for both batch learning with momentum and delta-bar-delta. The result supports using structural information to scale learning updates, with the approximate independence assumption providing the foundation for the proposed calculation.
neurips-1995-tempering-backpropagation-n.tldr: Structure-aware scaling of backpropagation updates yields more than a tenfold convergence speedup on the family-relations benchmark.

paragraphs: This paper derives temporal-difference learning for problems in which both time and state are continuous. The motivation is to make reinforcement learning applicable to physical control tasks and neurobiological modeling. A continuous formulation connects the learning rule directly to systems whose states evolve continuously.

The authors also derive an optimal nonlinear feedback-control law from derivatives of the value function. The critic represents information about paths toward the goal, while the actor uses a nonlinear feedback controller to determine behavior. Both are implemented with radial basis function networks, linking the continuous mathematical formulation to neural representations that can be used in the task.

The algorithms are tested by swinging a pendulum upright with limited torque. The abstract reports successful implementations of both actor and critic. The torque constraint makes the demonstration a constrained control problem, and the contribution combines value learning with a way to derive control actions from that value representation in continuous time and state.
neurips-1995-temporal-difference-learnin.tldr: Continuous-time temporal-difference learning and value-derived feedback control are demonstrated on a torque-limited pendulum swing-up task.

paragraphs: This paper modifies a multilayer perceptron so that its connections can process temporal information. The Gamma MLP replaces ordinary synaptic weights with gamma filters and associated gain terms throughout the network. A connection therefore has a filtering role as well as a gain, extending the network's treatment of signals across time.

The authors derive gradient-descent update equations for the architecture and apply it to speech-phoneme recognition. They examine two design choices: placing gamma filters in every layer and including synaptic gains. Both improve performance, showing that the placement of temporal processing and the accompanying gains each contribute to the reported results.

The Gamma MLP is compared with time-delay neural networks, Back-Tsoi FIR and IIR multilayer perceptrons, and a local approximation scheme. The authors report a substantial reduction in error rates. The contribution combines a trainable temporal architecture with evidence that distributing filters through all layers, together with gain terms, improves phoneme recognition in the comparisons presented.
neurips-1995-the-gamma-mlp-for-speech-ph.tldr: Replacing MLP weights with gamma filters and gains throughout the network substantially reduces speech-phoneme recognition errors.
